question: Explain the bias-variance trade-off and how underfitting and overfitting relate to it.
reference_answer: High bias occurs when a model is too simple to capture underlying patterns, causing high training and test error (underfitting). High variance occurs when a model memorizes training noise, achieving low training error but poor generalization on unseen data (overfitting). Regularization, cross-validation, and more training data help balance the two.
expected_concepts: high bias underfitting|high variance overfitting|generalization error|regularization|cross-validation

question: Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced classification datasets, and which metrics should you use instead?
reference_answer: If 99% of samples are negative, a trivial classifier predicting all negatives achieves 99% accuracy while missing every positive case. Instead, evaluate Precision (fraction of predicted positives that are correct), Recall (fraction of actual positives caught), F1-score, and Precision-Recall AUC (PR-AUC) alongside the confusion matrix.

question: What is the difference between supervised, unsupervised, and self-supervised learning?
reference_answer: Supervised learning trains on labeled input-output pairs (e.g., classification, regression). Unsupervised learning discovers hidden structure in unlabeled data (e.g., clustering, PCA). Self-supervised learning derives supervisory targets directly from unlabeled data itself (such as next-token prediction or masked language modeling) to learn rich representations.
expected_concepts: labeled training data|clustering and dimensionality reduction|pretext tasks|next-token prediction|representation learning

question: How does gradient descent work, and why are optimizers like Adam often preferred over vanilla SGD?
reference_answer: Gradient descent iteratively updates parameters in the opposite direction of the loss gradient scaled by a learning rate. Vanilla SGD uses a single global learning rate and can oscillate in steep ravines. Adam combines momentum (first-moment estimate) with per-parameter adaptive learning rates (second-moment estimate), converging faster with less manual tuning.
expected_concepts: loss gradient|learning rate|momentum|adaptive per-parameter scaling|convergence stability

question: Explain how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) works and why it reduces LLM hallucinations.
reference_answer: RAG converts documents into dense vector embeddings stored in a vector database. At query time, it embeds the user query, retrieves the top-k semantically similar chunks, and injects them as grounded context into the LLM prompt. This anchors answers in verifiable, up-to-date facts without retraining model weights.
expected_concepts: dense vector embeddings|semantic top-k retrieval|grounded prompt context|hallucination reduction|knowledge freshness

question: Explain cosine similarity versus Euclidean distance when comparing text embeddings.
reference_answer: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, making it invariant to vector magnitude and focused strictly on semantic direction. Euclidean distance measures straight-line distance in vector space and is sensitive to magnitude; when embeddings are L2-normalized to unit length, maximizing cosine similarity is equivalent to minimizing Euclidean distance.
expected_concepts: angle vs magnitude|semantic direction|L2 normalization|vector space distance|embedding comparison

question: Explain the self-attention mechanism in Transformers and why multi-head attention is used.
reference_answer: Self-attention projects each token into Query, Key, and Value vectors, computes scaled dot-product attention weights softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k))V, and lets every token attend directly to all other tokens in parallel. Multi-head attention runs several independent attention projections simultaneously so the model can capture syntactic, positional, and semantic relationships in different subspaces.
expected_concepts: Query Key Value projections|scaled dot-product attention|sqrt(d_k) scaling|parallel token context|multi-head subspaces

question: How would you evaluate a RAG pipeline end to end, separating retrieval quality from generation quality?
reference_answer: Evaluate retrieval independently using Recall@k, Precision@k, MRR, or NDCG on an annotated query-passage set. Evaluate generation using faithfulness/groundedness (whether claims are supported by retrieved chunks), answer relevance, and agreement with human rubric scores (Pearson/Spearman correlation and MAE), while also monitoring latency.
expected_concepts: Recall@k and MRR|faithfulness and groundedness|answer relevance|human score correlation|end-to-end latency
